notes:
Here are my notes on Philippians 4. Two things limited them. First, I couldn't open any page on the Catholic/Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) or the modern-scholarship sites (netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org), so those sections have little in them. The few Church Father views below come to us second-hand, through Protestant commentaries. Second, the Enduring Word page cut off partway through v. 17, so for vv. 17–23 I mostly used Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) and other sources.

---

## v. 1
- **Traditional reading:** "Therefore" points back to the promise of resurrection at the end of ch. 3. The word for "crown" is *stephanos*, the prize given to a winning athlete, not a king's crown. The Philippians were Paul's trophy. You can only "stand firm" when you are "in the Lord." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- JFB says Paul repeats "beloved" so that his love for them would move them to obey. The "crown" belongs to the day of the Lord. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- Pulpit Commentary: "so" can mean "as ye have us for an example; or perhaps, as becomes citizens of the heavenly commonwealth". Paul uses the same verb in 1:27, also tied to citizenship. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/philippians-4.html
- Matthew Henry reads it as: keep standing as you have been, right to the end. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Phl/Phl_004.cfm

## v. 2
- **Traditional reading:** These two women apparently caused a quarrel in the church. Paul doesn't take sides or try to settle the issue; he just tells them to be of the same mind in the Lord. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- Paul repeats "I urge" for each woman separately, as if to show complete fairness. Being "in the Lord" is what unites Christians, so believers quarrelling is a contradiction. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- Matthew Henry suggests the dispute might have been a civil matter, even a lawsuit, or a difference of religious opinion. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Phl/Phl_004.cfm
- **Minority views on who they were:** Adam Clarke thought it more likely that Euodias was a woman, and Syntyche a man, and probably the husband of Euodias, and that Syntyche is the "yokefellow" of v. 3. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-2.html. Barclay mentions an old guess that they were the Philippian jailer and his wife. He rejects it because Euodia is a woman's name. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/philippians-4.html

## v. 3
- **Traditional reading:** The "true companion" was meant to help the two women make peace. Clement of Rome was a well-known church leader, but since Clement was a common Roman name, we can't know if this is him. Having your name in the Book of Life is the greatest honour there is. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- **Who was the yokefellow?** Suggestions include Timothy, Silas, the chief bishop of Philippi, or a man actually named "Synzygus" ("yokefellow"). JFB says it was "certainly not" Paul's wife. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html. Pulpit says Chrysostom took it to be the husband of one of the women, which it thinks unlikely; others suggest Lydia. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/philippians-4.html
- **Clement:** Alford thought he was a Philippian, but Origen identifies the Clement here with the bishop of Rome. JFB adds a Protestant point: Clement's surviving letter to Corinth says nothing about the supremacy of Peter's see. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/4-3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- **Where traditions differ (the women's role):**
  - JFB (Anglican/Presbyterian authors) thinks they taught other women, "of course not in public preaching" (citing 1 Tim 2:11–12). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
  - Benson (Methodist) says the Greek word means they "wrestled, or contended together" with Paul. It speaks of opposition, danger and hard work, not preaching. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/4-3.htm
  - A writer quoted on Precept Austin calls the word "they agonised by my side" a tribute to women. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_41-7
- **The Book of Life:**
  - The Geneva Study Bible (Reformed) says it holds the names of his elect.
  - Benson (Methodist) says it holds the names of all true believers.
  - Source for both: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/4-3.htm
  - JFB compares it to the citizen rolls of ancient free cities. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html

## v. 4
- **Traditional reading:** Joy runs all through this letter. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: happy people neither give nor take offence easily, so joy in the Lord cures quarrels (tying back to v. 2). This joy rests on confidence that God is in control, not on optimism. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- "Always" means even in the middle of hardship. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- Barclay: joy has nothing to do with material things or with a man's outward circumstances. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-13.html

## v. 5
- **"Gentleness" (*epieikeia*):** Other versions say forbearance, patience or magnanimity. It describes someone who lets the Lord fight his battles. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- JFB: it means not pressing your rights to the limit. God is the model, since he doesn't hold us to the full strictness of his law. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- **"The Lord is near":** Both Guzik and JFB read this as Christ's soon return. Because the Lord will judge, it isn't our job to deal harshly with others. — same two URLs
- Pulpit suggests this may also be aimed at the Euodia–Syntyche quarrel. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/philippians-4.html

## v. 6
- **Traditional reading:** "Be anxious for nothing" is a command, not an option. "Everything" is a fit subject for prayer. "Prayer" is the general word; "supplication" means asking for something specific. Thanksgiving keeps prayer from turning into complaint. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- JFB quotes Bengel: worry and prayer are as opposed as fire and water. We should give thanks in good times and bad. Nothing is too big or too small to bring to God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html

## v. 7
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik separates peace *from* God, peace *with* God, and the peace *of* God. This verse is about the last of these. It goes beyond what we can understand, so it has to be experienced. "Guard" is a military word. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- JFB: God's peace keeps the heart like a garrisoned fortress (compare Isaiah 26:3). We are kept safe "in" Christ Jesus. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html

## v. 8
- **Traditional reading:** These things are both the fruit and the food of a mind guarded by God's peace. Guzik ties the verse to Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 10:5. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- JFB notes that "virtue" was the standard word of pagan moral philosophy and appears only here in Paul. Paul's point is not to despise anything good in itself, as long as it keeps its proper place. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- Barclay on "lovely": the Greek *prosphilēs* means that which calls forth love, and "winsome" is the best translation. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-13.html

## v. 9
- **Traditional reading:** Paul could honestly offer himself as an example. Those who obey have not only the peace *of* God but the God *of* peace with them. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html

## v. 10
- **Traditional reading:** This refers to the gift Epaphroditus brought. The Philippians had always cared but had no opportunity to show it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- JFB: "revived" pictures a tree sprouting again in spring. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- Sam Storms (charismatic): "at last" implies a long gap since their last support. — https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/philippians-410-13

## v. 11
- **Traditional reading:** The Greek word for "content" literally means self-sufficient. JFB says Christianity raised it from the Stoic's proud self-sufficiency to the Christian's sufficiency in God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- Contentment has to be learned; it doesn't come naturally. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- Contentment does not mean complacency; Christians may still work to improve their circumstances. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_411-131
- Storms: this is not laziness or fatalism. Paul's joy simply didn't depend on how much he owned. — https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/philippians-410-13

## v. 12
- **Traditional reading:** "I have learned the secret" literally means being initiated into a mystery. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: many know how to be brought low but not how to abound. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- Matthew Henry: the temptations of having plenty are not less than those of affliction and want. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-13.html

## v. 13
- **Traditional reading:** "All things" is limited by the context. Poole says not to understand it absolutely, but restrictively, of using both good times and hard times well. — https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-13.html
- Calvin: Paul adds "through Christ" so his claim won't be taken as pride. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-13.html
- **Text and grammar:** The best manuscripts leave out the word "Christ," and the phrase is better read "in him who strengthens me." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/4-13.htm. The preposition is "in," which points to union with Christ. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_411-131
- **A broader reading:** Ellicott accepts that the verse is first about bearing hardship. Even so, the universal extension of the maxim beyond the immediate occasion and context is not inadmissible. — https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-13.html. Constable likewise says Christ can enable much more than contentment. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-13.html
- **Debated popular use:**
  - Ligonier (David Briones) says the verse is a statement of contentment, not a promise to reach every dream. There is absolutely no room for a health, wealth, and prosperity interpretation of this text. — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/what-does-philippians-4-13-mean
  - GotQuestions directly contrasts this verse with prosperity teaching. — https://www.gotquestions.org/I-can-do-all-things-through-Christ.html
  - Guzik (from a Calvary Chapel / charismatic-friendly background) warns against a "triumphalist" or "super-Christian" reading. He pairs the verse with John 15:5. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/

## v. 14
- **Traditional reading:** Paul doesn't want them to think he looks down on their gift. Giving does more good for the giver than for the receiver. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/
- By sympathising and sending a gift, they made themselves sharers in his suffering. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html

## vv. 15–16
- **Traditional reading:** "Giving and receiving" is account language: all the giving was on their side, all the receiving on his. JFB's lesson from "you only": don't wait for others before doing good. Even in Thessalonica they sent help more than once. JFB also links this to 2 Corinthians 11:8–9, following Paley. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html

## v. 17
- **Traditional reading:** Paul wants spiritual "fruit" credited to their account for the day of reward. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- The Bridgeway commentary describes their gifts as like an investment with God, who, as their banker, will add interest to their account. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-13.html

## v. 18
- **Traditional reading:** "Fragrant offering" comes from the incense burned with Old Testament sacrifices. The gift was really given to God (compare Matthew 25:40; Hebrews 13:16). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html

## v. 19
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Ellicott: "my God" is emphatic, meaning the God you served by serving me. "All your needs" covers both spiritual and physical needs. — https://biblehub.com/philippians/4-19.htm
  - JFB: Paul is saying "My Master will fully repay you; I cannot." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
  - Calvin: the promise is not only about the next life but even in respect of the necessities of the present life. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-19.html
- **Different emphases among Protestant teachers:**
  - Barnes (Presbyterian) is optimistic in practice: The benevolent are not usually poor. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/4-19.htm
  - Krell, quoted on Precept Austin, makes the promise conditional on giving: faithful givers can expect their financial needs met; non-givers shouldn't. The same page also insists the verse is not a blank check. It is not a promise of prosperity. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_419-23
  - Constable: God meets needs, not "greeds." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-19.html
- **Prosperity teaching (critique):** "Contending for the Faith" says many twist this verse into a guarantee of health and wealth; God supplies needs, not wants. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-19.html. A Bible Hub article argues the verse undercuts the prosperity gospel. It reports that Chrysostom said God gives what is needful, not superfluous, and that Augustine linked the verse to Matthew 6:33. — https://biblehub.com/q/Philippians_4_19_and_prosperity_gospel.htm

## v. 20
- **Traditional reading:** Better translated "the glory": the glory for both their gift and God's repayment belongs to him, not to us. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- The final "Amen" is Paul's word of agreement with all he has written. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-4/

## v. 21
- **Traditional reading:** "Greet every saint" means each one individually. JFB thinks "the brothers with me" may be Jewish believers rather than close colleagues, since Timothy was Paul's only close friend there (2:20). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html

## v. 22
- **Traditional reading:** "Caesar's household" probably means "slaves and freedmen attached to the palace" (Lightfoot), not the emperor's relatives. Lightfoot showed the term covered a huge staff in Rome and the provinces. Burial inscriptions match names in Romans 16. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/4-22.htm
- Calvin sees it as a sign of God's mercy that the gospel reached Nero's court. Clarke cites Jerome's claim that Paul converted many in Caesar's family. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/4-22.html
- Pulpit thinks Chrysostom's explanation for singling them out is "somewhat fanciful." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/4-22.htm
- **Where was Paul writing from?** Traditionally Rome; GotQuestions and MacArthur both read the verse as pointing there. — https://www.gotquestions.org/prison-epistles.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/macarthur_john/bible-introductions/philippians-intro.cfm. The Holman Bible Dictionary says an Ephesus origin also has much in its favor, because a provincial governor's residence could also be called "Caesar's household." — https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hbd/p/philippians.html. Bible.org lists three options: Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea. — https://bible.org/seriespage/introduction-background-and-outline-philippians

## v. 23
- **Text:** (KJV: "with you all. Amen") JFB says the oldest manuscripts read "with your spirit" and leave out "Amen." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/philippians-4.html
- I found no further comment on this verse.

---

**Gaps that need another round:** Catholic and Orthodox readings (for example, Catholic views on Clement in v. 3), NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey articles, and Lutheran and Wesley's own notes (wesley.nnu.edu) on vv. 3 and 13.
